page: Amazon Web Services r6gd.large is a memory-optimized server instance powered by the AWS Graviton processor family. It features 2 dedicated physical cores on the arm64 architecture utilizing the Neoverse-N1 model running at 2.5 GHz. The hardware configuration includes 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per core. Local storage is provided via a bundled 118 GB NVMe SSD instance store volume, and baseline network bandwidth is rated at 1 Gbps.

Benchmark results indicate moderate single-core performance alongside weaker multi-core and memory bandwidth metrics. The stress-ng single-core CPU test scored 1519.49, falling into the average category, while the multi-core score of 3012.08 is categorized as weak. Memory bandwidth tests showed 117.2 GB/sec for cached small blocks and 36.85 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. The instance achieved 2.48 million operations per second on Redis SET operations and a Passmark database operations score of 1309.2, reflecting its positioning for memory-bound but compute-light workloads.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the r6gd.large offers a dense memory profile and local NVMe storage on an ARM-based architecture, which typically reduces power and resource overhead compared to x86 equivalents. However, the trade-off lies in its lower compute and memory bandwidth performance, as evidenced by poor scores in multi-threaded decompression, software compilation, and LLM inference. This server is suited for memory-intensive workloads with moderate CPU requirements, such as caching layers, lightweight database hosting, and local-storage-dependent web serving.

Performance benchmarks show average single-core CPU capabilities (stress-ng score of 1519.49) but weaker multi-core and memory bandwidth results, such as a Geekbench multi-core score of 1753.0 and 36.85 GB/sec uncached read bandwidth. Qualitatively, the instance offers a cost-efficient memory-to-vCPU ratio and local storage on energy-efficient ARM architecture, though it presents compute-performance trade-offs. It is suited for memory-intensive, low-compute workloads like caching layers, lightweight database operations, and static web serving.
